newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt signs work pact with unions, employers.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt signs work pact with unions, employers.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi signed a wide-ranging labour pact with unions and business leaders late on Tuesday in a deal aimed at cutting Italy's army of unemployed.
The long-awaited accord includes a reduction in the working week, incentives for people starting up their own businesses, tax breaks on research and encouragement for training schemes.

It also promises to kick start a major programme of infrastrucure projects worth some 40 trillion lire ($26.4 billion) which was largely frozen following the "Tangentopoli" (bribesville) corruption scandals of the early 1990s.

"With this accord we will have new, concrete policies for the labour market to tackle the employment emergency," Prodi told a news conference after signing the deal. "It will have an immediate impact on the jobless total," he added.
According to latest data from the national statisitics office Istat, 2.82 million people, or 12.3 percent of the work force, were unemployed in Italy in April.

The problem was especially acute in the underdeveloped south, where the jobless total was 22.2 percent, with 57.3 percent of people between 15-24 looking for work. In the rich north, the overall unemployment rate was just 6.5 percent.
Union leaders said the main thrust of Tuesday's pact was to launch training projects and create work in the poorer south.
"This is the first accord in Europe which defines an active employment policy," said Sergio D'Antoni, the leader of Italy's second largest union, the Cisl.

Italy's centre-left government has put the fight against unemployment at the centre of its agenda and has been negotiating with unions and the employers' federation Confindustria since July on the labour pact.
However Prodi's room for manoeuvre is limited by tight budgetary restraints, with the government fighting to curb the state deficit and slash back public spending.
Confindustria leader Giorgio Fossa said that although he had signed Tuesday's agreement, he had reservations about it and hoped Prodi would introduce more generous fiscal incentives.
"This is just a first step but not the whole picture," Fossa told reporters. "We signed (the deal) even if the measures aimed at encouraging development are only partly worked out."
The main points of the labour pact include:
-- Reduction in the legal working week to 40 hours from 48 with fiscal breaks for companies which adopt shorter working weeks along with disincentives to cut the use of overtime.
-- The minimum age at which people can leave school will be raised to 16 from the present 14. Everyone up to the age of 18 will be guaranteed a place at school.

-- Major infrastructure programmes to be re-launched, with private investment encouraged and planning rules simplified. The government expects the various schemes will create 50,000 jobs. The government has pledged to start work on some of the projects, including a second Florence-to-Bologna motorway and high speed train links, by December.
-- Incentives for young or unemployed people who start their own businesses and a tax break for firms investing in research.
-- Apprenticehips introduced in all sectors for people aged between 16-24. This age limit rises to 26 in the south. $1 = 1,515 lire
